items.text: Go outside too. Go where it's quiet.
items.q: Maman urges her grown son not to stay home all the time. Does this sound natural from a mother?
before: – Oh, that's good. Mm-hm, you order and they bring it to you. But Amir-jan, don't stay home all the time.

items.text: There was typhoid, for example, or tuberculosis, or measles. They called those deadly. Hmm, even those didn't kill this many. Or cholera, for example.
items.q: An elderly mother lists old deadly diseases her family spoke of. Does this sound natural?
before: …came, television said two people out of every hundred, and now it says ten percent. By God, it's so unfair. Someone sneezes on one side of the street, and a person on the other side catches it and dies. I'd never seen or heard of such a thing. Even Bibi's generation never spoke of anything like it.

items.text: – Mahboub, this thing they're saying on the news, Ameroca ...
items.q: Maman says 'Ameroca' for America on purpose. Does it read as her slip, not a typo?
before: …left the house at the far end of the courtyard and crossed the courtyard in nine steps, the happiness of the new discovery still bright in my heart. When I entered the hall from the courtyard, Maman was lying in front of the television. She had both hands on her stomach and was saying to Mahboubeh:

items.q: Maman says 'Ayzheimer' for Alzheimer on purpose. Does it read as her slip, not a typo?
before: – Maman, there is a disease that slowly shuts down the muscles. It's a very bad disease.
Maman said:

items.text: In the end Mahboub called, and they came in an amublace and took Naney away.
items.q: Maman says 'amublace' for ambulance on purpose. Does it read as her slip, not a typo?
before: …can't hear and has no idea what's going on, but I'd told Naney several times: Haaj Khanom, you sit out in the alley, you'll catch Covid, God forbid. That only made them sit out there even more. But Amir, Naney's chest was rattling so badly. I told Mahboub and the others: "Kids, this is Covid."

items.q: Maman, hard of hearing, catches only the end of 'womanizer'. Does her puzzled question read naturally?
before: – He wasn't a womanizer either.
Maman says:

items.q: Maman, hard of hearing, catches only the end of the series title 'Tears and Smiles'. Does her question read naturally?
before: – Kids, should I download Tears and Smiles so we can watch it tonight?
Maman turns her head and says:

items.text: – But he fucked it up. Eagle Eye says peer-to-peer; Taverny says Eldie-to-Eldie.
items.q: Amir misheard 'peer-to-peer' as 'Pir-to-pir'; pir is Persian for elder, hence his nicknames. Does Farid's punch line land?
before: – Pir-to-pir?
Hooman said:
– Send a salavat. Elder of the Tavern finally said something.
Farid said:

items.text: – Last night I could hear you ruminating. Too bad my Baba was asleep, otherwise I'd have gotten up and pulled every single sweet out of your throat.
items.q: Eskandar teases Hooman for secretly eating sweets at night, like a cow chewing cud. Does 'ruminating' make the joke land?
before: Eskandar turned toward Hooman and said:

items.text: – Here. Listen to this. For-for God's sake, listen. "The wine there is real no metaphor." This is the same thing.
items.q: This Hafez line has no comma on purpose, so it can be read two opposite ways. Does that double meaning come through?
before: With trembling hands I flipped frantically through the ghazals, searching for the Hafez beit that, like the painting, as that other girl had said, would make us more shit-dizzy the deeper we sank into it. I wanted to show it to Niloofar.

items.q: The guard jokes that the surname Arasteh is the Persian word 'Araasteh' (neat) with one letter trimmed. Does the joke come through?
before: I enter the university again. I have gone only a few steps when I hear the guard's voice behind me.
– Mr. Arasteh.
I turn my head toward him.

items.text: – Forgiven. The whole boulevard is yours.
items.q: Niloofar forgives him, then playfully grants him the whole boulevard too (in Persian, forgive and give are one word). Does it read naturally?
before: – Come on. No cheating. Last time you chose. Tonight it's my turn.
– Sorry, I wasn't thinking.

items.text: – What the hell's wrong with you this time, getting it up at us, Alain Dickon?
items.q: Eskandar has called them all cows; Hooman's comeback carries a crude sexual double meaning. Does it land naturally?
before: – Understanding is a good thing. I say you're cows and sheep, and you get upset.
Hooman said:

items.text: – Vwoooom! Baba, Baba, wiw you buy me dis big dolly?
items.q: A toddler asks her father for a doll in baby talk. Does it read as a small child's speech, not typos?
before: …lamp that destroyed that soothing, dark-hued silence, yet shed too little light to guide me. A blinking lamp in the hand of a girl whose front door was a color I could never place in the box of colored pencils. A little girl comes vrooming over and stops beside me. She looks at the toys. She says:

items.text: – Ohhh, objectively, nice work. They saw the red and all their body hair fell right out, objectively.
items.q: This Persian image means they got a sudden fright. Is the meaning of 'all their body hair fell right out' clear?
before: Again came the sound of three receding footsteps. Sajad's voice came:

items.text: – I'd give anything for you, Nini-jan. Your mind works so well.
items.q: Amir praises his mother, whom the family affectionately calls Nini, with a Persian endearment. Does 'I'd give anything for you' sound warm?
before: – Amir, when Taghi died, his mother came to the door and said to Maman: we don't know what to tell people. I mean, if we say he'd been drinking strong homemade aragh and had syncope, it would be a terrible disgrace. Then Maman told her: just say he caught Covid.
I say:
